standard.title: Locate and Organise Information
standard.description: locate, select and organise information and data from a range of sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can locate, collect and organise information from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats (AC9HS6S02). At Year 7, the demand shifts to selecting from a wider range of source types — including government and NGO websites and digital tools — and to organising using more specialised formats such as tables, graphs and visual displays.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate, select and organise information and data from a range of sources.

nodes.label: Locating sources using targeted search
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate relevant economics and business sources using targeted search techniques, including advanced search functions.
nodes.minimum_width: Locate two relevant sources for an economic topic using a search engine; describe the search terms used.
nodes.typical_width: Locate online sources using targeted search techniques — advanced search functions ('define: market'), targeted criteria ('allintext: successful Australian entrepreneurs'), government department and NGO websites; explain how the search approach was tailored to the question.
wider: Compare the results of a broad versus a targeted search for the same economic topic — evaluating which approach yields more relevant, reliable sources
Collaborate with a peer to exchange information online with an entrepreneur or industry contact to gather primary source data
Explore how to locate First Nations economic and business sources — including community organisations, AIATSIS and First Nations business directories — and evaluate their reliability and relevance
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot locate sources reliably using targeted search, their entire information base will be too broad, biased or unreliable to support a meaningful investigation. Weak locating cascades through selection and organisation phases.

response_modes.reason: Targeted search is a precision skill that degrades when students default to broad keyword searches. Targeted practice with economics-specific search techniques — including 'define:' and 'allintext:' operators — builds reliable searching habits that carry through the investigation.

success_criteria: Locates at least two relevant sources for an economic topic
Describes the search terms or strategy used and explains why they were chosen

nodes.label: Selecting relevant information
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select information and data from sources by evaluating its relevance to their investigation question.
nodes.minimum_width: Select two pieces of information from a source and explain how each helps answer the investigation question.
nodes.typical_width: Select relevant information and data from a range of sources by applying the question 'How will this data or information help answer my question?'; distinguish relevant from irrelevant information; apply to websites of government departments and non-government organisations.
wider: Evaluate conflicting information from two sources on the same economic issue — explaining which is more useful and why
Practise selective use of a complex multi-variable dataset: identify only the variables needed to answer a specific question and exclude the rest
Evaluate the relevance and reliability of information provided by an entrepreneur contacted online, and identify what follow-up questions would strengthen the data
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish relevant from irrelevant information will collect indiscriminately, producing disorganised and unfocused responses. The selection criterion — 'does this help answer my question?' — is the discipline that makes subsequent organisation and interpretation meaningful.

response_modes.reason: Students need a practical decision rule they can apply at source level: for each piece of information, ask 'Does this directly help answer my question?' Scaffold this as a routine check, not a post-hoc judgement.

success_criteria: Selects at least two pieces of information from a source with a stated reason for relevance
Discards or sets aside information identified as not relevant to the investigation question

nodes.label: Organising data using appropriate formats
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can organise information and data into appropriate formats — tables, graphs, visual displays — using digital tools.
nodes.minimum_width: Organise selected information into one appropriate format (table or graph) using a digital tool; explain why the format suits the data.
nodes.typical_width: Organise data into appropriate formats using specialised digital tools — tables, graphs, visual displays; select the format that best suits the type and purpose of the data; apply to economics data (e.g. income data, business type counts, consumer trend data).
wider: Organise multi-variable data (e.g. employment type by age group) into a format that makes the relevant relationship visible — comparing multiple format options before selecting
Curate a visual display combining data from multiple sources — practising how to integrate information from different formats into a coherent organised product
Use a digital tool to organise qualitative data (e.g. interview responses from an entrepreneur) into a structured format suitable for analysis

response_modes.reason: Format selection requires practice with real data across multiple types. Students who default to one format (usually a table) need explicit experience with graphs and visual displays to build a repertoire of organisation strategies.

success_criteria: Organises selected information into an appropriate format using a digital tool
Explains why the chosen format suits the data type
